The plan model

Source: vignettes/plan_concepts.Rmd
plan_concepts.Rmd
library(mediaplanr)

mediaplanr is small on purpose. Most of the decisions that shaped it were about what to leave out, and those decisions are not visible from the function reference. This vignette covers the model behind the functions — the ideas that, misunderstood, lead to using the package incorrectly in ways nothing will catch.

vignette("getting_started") covers what to type.

A plan holds intent

Every row of a plan is planned spend — what was intended — including for weeks that have already passed. It is never a record of what happened.

That distinction matters because reality diverges from intent constantly: under-delivery, over-delivery, a partner that never went live. Actualised spend and attributed results live in a decomp — the output of a media-mix model — which this package does not hold and does not read.

So a row for a past week is still intent. Revising it is an ordinary thing to do: you are correcting what the plan said, not rewriting history.

p <- media_plan_from_df(
  data.frame(
    week          = as.Date(c("2026-01-05", "2026-01-05")),
    channel       = c("TV", "Search"),
    planned_spend = c(50000, 20000)
  ),
  grain = "channel", time = "week",
  name  = "A plan whose weeks are long past"
)

# Editing a week from January is not special, and nothing objects.
build_scenario(p, edits = list(target = list(channel = "TV"), scale = 1.5),
               name = "revised")@data
#>         week channel planned_spend
#> 1 2026-01-05      TV         75000
#> 2 2026-01-05  Search         20000

Credits are not intent

Agency workbooks often carry negative rows: a make-good credit, a rebate, a partner refunding an under-delivered week. A plan refuses them:

media_plan_from_df(
  data.frame(week = as.Date("2026-01-05"), channel = c("TV", "TV credit"),
             planned_spend = c(50000, -4000)),
  grain = "channel", time = "week", name = "With a credit row"
)
#> Error in `MediaPlan()`:
#> ! <mediaplanr::MediaPlan> object is invalid:
#> - 'planned_spend' must be non-negative.

That is deliberate. A credit is billing reconciliation, not something anyone planned to buy, so it is not a line item. Decide which of two things it is:

  • It changes planned media — the credit was reinvested, or the line is genuinely buying less. Net it into that line’s planned_spend before import, so the plan says what is now intended.
  • It does not — the media runs as planned and only the invoice changes. Keep it in a separate adjustments table outside the plan, and reconcile the two where billing is done.

A plan is blind to past and future

This follows from the above, and it is the point most likely to be missed.

“Historical”, “future”, “under-delivery”, “over-delivery” are not properties of a plan. They only exist for a pairing of a plan with a decomp that reports actuals through some date. A plan on its own cannot tell you which of its rows are in the past, because that depends entirely on which decomp you hold it against — and that boundary moves every time the decomp is refreshed.

Consequences you can see in the API:

  • There is no historical_spend column. An earlier revision had one; it was removed. Freezing a moving boundary into the data guarantees it goes stale.
  • No through-date is stored on a MediaPlan.
  • Nothing stops you editing a row for a past week.

The one pairing operation the package provides is check_coverage():

plan <- media_plan_from_df(
  data.frame(
    week          = rep(as.Date(c("2026-03-02", "2026-04-06")), each = 2),
    channel       = c("TV", "Search", "TV", "Search"),
    partner       = c("NBC", "Google", "NBC", "Google"),
    planned_spend = c(30000, 20000, 35000, 25000)
  ),
  grain = c("channel", "partner"), time = "week",
  name  = "Q2 plan"
)

# What the model measured, historically.
decomp <- data.frame(
  channel = c("TV", "Search", "Audio"),
  partner = c("NBC", "Google", "Spotify"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

missing <- check_coverage(plan, decomp, through = as.Date("2026-03-15"))
#> Warning: the plan is missing 1 line item(s) present in the decomp: Audio |
#> Spotify
missing
#> [1] "Audio | Spotify"

Three things about that check are deliberate:

It runs decomp → plan, not the reverse. Every line item the model measured should appear in the plan’s pre-through-date rows. The opposite direction is never flagged: the future portion of a plan is expected to introduce new partners and tactics.

It is scoped by through, on overlap. A row is considered when any part of its in-market period falls before that date, since the decomp only knows about history. A decomp reporting through a Wednesday has measured part of the week that began on the Monday, so that line item should be expected in the plan.

The comparison is against the row’s real period, not the bare week value, so it follows a flight that starts mid-week:

midweek <- media_plan_from_flights(
  data.frame(channel = "TV", flight_start = as.Date("2026-04-08"),
             flight_end = as.Date("2026-04-19"), planned_spend = 100),
  grain = "channel", name = "Starts on the Wednesday"
)

# the buy was not live on the 7th, so nothing is in scope to check
tryCatch(check_coverage(midweek, data.frame(channel = "TV"),
                        through = as.Date("2026-04-07")),
         warning = function(w) conditionMessage(w))
#> [1] "no plan rows are in market before 2026-04-07; not checked."

Being in scope says the decomp saw part of a buy, not much of it: a long flight that began the day before through qualifies on a single measured day. That is the right answer for the question being asked — should this line item appear in the plan? — but it is not a statement about delivery.

It warns rather than errors. Both artifacts are individually valid; it is their pairing that disagrees. An app should surface that and let the user resolve it, not refuse to load a perfectly well-formed plan.

Extent is not a boundary

A plan does know one thing about its own dates: which ones it covers. That is its extent, and it is not the same species of fact as a through-date.

c(plan@flight_start, plan@flight_end)
#> [1] "2026-03-02" "2026-04-12"
plan@flight_days
#> [1] 42

The discriminating question is: can this value change without the plan changing? A decomp’s through-date can — it moves every refresh, and the plan sits still while it does. A flight window cannot: it is a pure function of @data. So one is an argument to check_coverage() and the other is a property of the plan.

That test is also what keeps the class from re-growing the things that were removed. historical_spend, weeks_remaining, is_active, pct_delivered all fail it — each needs either Sys.Date() or a decomp — so none of them belongs here, however convenient they would be.

Note that @flight_end is the last day the plan is in market, not the last week start stored in @data. A week is seven days of spend, so a plan whose final week begins on a Monday runs through the Sunday after it.

That last point about warnings is the one exception to the package’s general strictness. Structural problems — negative spend, duplicate rows, a time column that is neither a Date nor a moment — are hard errors, so an invalid plan cannot exist:

media_plan_from_df(
  data.frame(week = as.Date("2026-07-06"), channel = c("TV", "TV"), planned_spend = c(1, 2)),
  grain = "channel", time = "week", name = "duplicated"
)
#> Error in `MediaPlan()`:
#> ! <mediaplanr::MediaPlan> object is invalid:
#> - @data has duplicate rows at grain (channel, week): TV | 2026-07-06. One row per grain cell is required.

Time is not optional

Every plan is planned against a calendar, so @time_col is required. Two properties carry the whole time axis:

  • @time_col names the column a row is dated by.
  • @time_basis says what one of its values covers — "day", "week", "month", or "instant" for a buy placed at a specific moment.

Everything temporal is derived from those two plus the flight a row belongs to: the flight window, check_coverage()’s scope, calendarize(), pacing. Nothing stores a period, so nothing can disagree about one.

The basis is inferred from the column when you do not declare it — month starts read as monthly, dates that all fall on one weekday as weekly, anything else as daily, and a POSIXct column always as moments. Declare it when the guess would be wrong: a single month of a monthly plan looks exactly like a single week.

weeks <- media_plan_from_df(
  data.frame(week = as.Date(c("2026-04-06", "2026-04-13")),
             channel = "TV", planned_spend = c(30, 30)),
  grain = "channel", time = "week", name = "Weekly"
)
days <- media_plan_from_df(
  data.frame(day = as.Date(c("2026-04-06", "2026-04-07")),
             channel = "TV", planned_spend = c(30, 30)),
  grain = "channel", time = "day", name = "Daily"
)

c(weekly = weeks@flight_days, daily = days@flight_days)
#> weekly  daily 
#>     14      2

Two rows each, the same money, and different extents — because a weekly row is seven days of spend and a daily row is one.

A moment is the case for buys bought by the slot rather than for a period: a 30-second spot, an 8pm takeover, a half-hour sponsorship. The moment keys the row; the buy’s own flight says how long it runs. Author those the way a buyer states them — one row per slot, with a start and an end:

spots <- media_plan_from_flights(
  data.frame(
    channel   = "TV",
    programme = c("Grand Final", "Sunday Sponsorship"),
    flight_start = as.POSIXct(c("2026-04-06 20:00:00", "2026-04-12 20:00:00"),
                              tz = "UTC"),
    flight_end   = as.POSIXct(c("2026-04-06 20:00:30", "2026-04-12 20:30:00"),
                              tz = "UTC"),
    planned_spend = c(450000, 250000)
  ),
  grain = c("channel", "programme"), basis = "instant", name = "Launch spots"
)

spots@time_basis
#> [1] "instant"
flights(spots)[, c("programme", "flight_start", "flight_end", "n_periods")]
#>            programme        flight_start          flight_end n_periods
#> 1        Grand Final 2026-04-06 20:00:00 2026-04-06 20:00:30         1
#> 2 Sunday Sponsorship 2026-04-12 20:00:00 2026-04-12 20:30:00         1

One row per buy, because there is nothing to spread a slot across. Each row’s extent is its own: half a minute for the spot, half an hour for the sponsorship, and a bare moment with no flight is a point in time.

flight_window(spots)
#>                     start                       end 
#> "2026-04-06 20:00:00 UTC" "2026-04-12 20:30:00 UTC"
calendarize(spots, "day")   # onto a calendar by the day each spot airs
#>   channel          programme        day planned_spend
#> 1      TV        Grand Final 2026-04-06        450000
#> 2      TV Sunday Sponsorship 2026-04-12        250000

A moment is only a moment on some clock, so the clock is the plan’s: @tz. Declare it and a time given as a string means that time on the plan’s clock, wherever the code runs — 8pm in New York is not 8pm in London, and without a stated zone the machine parsing the edit would quietly decide which one you meant.

ny <- media_plan_from_df(
  data.frame(airs = "2026-02-08 20:00:00", channel = "TV", planned_spend = 1),
  grain = "channel", time = "airs", tz = "America/New_York", name = "NY spot"
)

ny@tz
#> [1] "America/New_York"
format(ny@data$airs, usetz = TRUE)
#> [1] "2026-02-08 20:00:00 EST"

It travels with the plan: JSON writes the instant in UTC so it cannot be read as a different moment, and @tz puts it back on the plan’s clock on the way in. A plan keyed by day, week or month has no clock to state, so @tz has no effect on one.

The time column is part of @grain, but you do not name it there: the constructors append it, and it always sits last.

spots@grain
#> [1] "channel"   "programme" "time"
line_item_grain(spots)
#> [1] "channel"   "programme"

That also means roll_up() never drops it. Rolling up aggregates over dimensions; aggregating over time is calendarize()’s job, and the two compose in either order.

Line item, grain, row

Three related ideas that are easy to conflate.

A line item is a channel / partner / tactic combination: the time-free identity of something you are buying. It is what a decomp constrains and what response models attach to.

The grain is the set of columns identifying a row. Every plan is keyed by time, so a row is a line item for one period — a week here, a day, a month or a moment elsewhere.

plan@grain              # what identifies a row
#> [1] "channel" "partner" "week"
line_item_grain(plan)   # what identifies a line item — the grain minus time
#> [1] "channel" "partner"

unique(line_item(plan@data, line_item_grain(plan)))
#> [1] "TV | NBC"        "Search | Google"

line_item() gives you the key for every row. For the distinct roster — one row per line item, with its total, its share of the plan’s rows and its own flight window — use line_item_summary():

line_item_summary(plan)
#>   channel partner       line_item planned_spend n_rows flight_start flight_end
#> 1      TV     NBC        TV | NBC         65000      2   2026-03-02 2026-04-12
#> 2  Search  Google Search | Google         45000      2   2026-03-02 2026-04-12

The grain values come back as columns rather than folded into the key, because that is the shape an edit target takes. So “which channels are in this plan?” is answered with values you can hand straight to build_scenario():

grain_values(plan, "channel")
#> [1] "Search" "TV"

There is deliberately no channels(). The package never privileges a column name — channel is simply a dimension you chose to key on, and another plan may key on media_type or vehicle. Naming your own column keeps that true, and a typo errors with the alternatives listed rather than returning nothing.

grain is deliberately ordered coarsest-first, because roll_up() treats it as a nesting. Dropping the rightmost column gives the next coarsest level — which is how you find a model for a line item that has none of its own:

roll_up(plan, c("channel", "week"))@data
#>   channel       week planned_spend
#> 1      TV 2026-03-02         30000
#> 2  Search 2026-03-02         20000
#> 3      TV 2026-04-06         35000
#> 4  Search 2026-04-06         25000

The package is a flat table at a configurable grain, not a nested object tree. A plan keyed by channel, by channel + partner, or by channel + partner + tactic + week is the same class at different grains.

Subplans: one number, one owner

A channel team plans its own detail at its own grain and cadence, and that detail rolls up into the topline everyone else looks at. A subplan is an ordinary MediaPlan held beneath one cell of another — composition, not a new class. What changes is the parent’s behaviour.

The subplan says which cell it backs through its data: its line item grain must contain the parent’s, and across the parent’s columns its rows hold one value — channel == "TV" throughout. So the cell is a fact in the table, not a string to be trusted, and reconciliation is the rollup the package already does.

tv <- media_plan_from_df(
  data.frame(week = as.Date("2026-07-06"), channel = "TV", partner = c("NBC", "ESPN"),
             planned_spend = c(70000, 50000)),
  grain = c("channel", "partner"), time = "week", name = "TV detail"
)
topline <- attach_subplan(roll_up(plan, "channel"), tv)
topline@data
#>   channel       week planned_spend
#> 1  Search 2026-03-02         20000
#> 2  Search 2026-04-06         25000
#> 3      TV 2026-07-06        120000

Attaching replaces the parent’s rows for that cell with the subplan’s rollup and makes them read-only. An edit that reaches them errors naming the right door — “channel TV is planned in a subplan; edit the subplan and re-attach” — so the topline cannot quietly drift from the detail beneath it. Re-attaching is the reconcile; there is no separate step. detach_subplan() releases the rows as ordinary editable rows, so detaching is never destructive.

A weekly parent re-cuts the subplan onto its own weeks with calendarize() first, so a daily flight or a Sunday-start plan lands correctly. roll_up() drops subplans (a rollup is a coarser view); build_scenario() carries them.

Flights are authored, weeks are held

A planner states a buy as a flight: in-market dates and a total. A plan is held, charted and edited as weeks. These are different things, and the package keeps them apart rather than picking one.

media_plan_from_flights() expands a flight onto the weekly rows @data already holds, so everything downstream sees the ordinary shape. flights() goes back the other way — and it is exact, never inferred:

weekly <- media_plan_from_df(
  data.frame(week = seq(as.Date("2026-04-06"), by = "week", length.out = 4),
             channel = "TV", planned_spend = rep(30000, 4)),
  grain = "channel", time = "week", name = "Four equal weeks"
)

nrow(flights(weekly))
#> [1] 0

Nothing is reported, because nothing was authored. Four consecutive 30,000 weeks are equally consistent with one 28-day flight, four weekly buys, or two fortnightly ones, and no rule can tell them apart. Guessing from runs of equal spend would be a guess presented as a fact — the failure mode the package refuses everywhere, the same reason a mistyped target errors instead of quietly matching nothing.

So the inverse works only because each buy’s identity is stored when it is authored. That identity survives derivation, which is what lets compare_scenarios(level = "flight") say a buy moved rather than showing an unexplained subtraction in one week and an addition in another.

One period per line item per week

A row is still one line item for one period, so two separate buys of the same line item cannot overlap the same week. That is an error naming the fix — add a column that tells them apart — rather than a silent sum that would merge two distinct buys.

It is also the price of keeping @data in the long weekly shape that makes the package pleasant to chart, edit and export. Making the flight the stored row instead was tried and rejected: @grain’s time member would become the flight start, so two scenarios that stage the same money differently would share no cells, and every reshaping would read as an add plus a drop rather than a move.

Pacing records shape, not history

A flight has a shape as well as a size. By default its spend is spread evenly across its days, so its weekly figures are whatever that gives — which for a buy with ragged ends is not four equal numbers:

ragged <- media_plan_from_flights(
  data.frame(channel = "OOH", flight_start = as.Date("2026-04-08"),
             flight_end = as.Date("2026-05-03"), planned_spend = 100000),
  grain = "channel", name = "Starts on a Wednesday"
)

ragged@data$planned_spend      # 5 days, then 7, 7, 7
#> [1] 19230.77 26923.08 26923.08 26923.07
flights(ragged)$pacing
#> [1] "even"

pacing is re-derived after every edit, not remembered. The question it answers is “do these rows still match an even spread?”, never “did somebody touch this?” — and that distinction is what makes it behave sensibly:

shape <- function(p) flights(p)$pacing

# scaling changes the buy's SIZE, not its shape
shape(build_scenario(ragged, edits = list(scale = 0.5), name = "half"))
#> [1] "even"

# a flat amount on every week cannot stay proportional to days, so it does
shape(build_scenario(ragged, edits = list(delta_each = 1000), name = "flat"))
#> [1] "custom"

Because it is derived rather than remembered, shaping a flight by hand and then shaping it back reports "even" again. There is no permanent mark.

A hand-shaped flight is never broken by the edit: it keeps its identity, so flights() still reports it whole and it can still be compared, moved and restaged as one buy. "custom" says the shape is no longer a rule, not that the buy has stopped being a buy.

The one place the package rewrites a number

Worth knowing because it is the exception to everything else here. When a flight is still evenly paced, its rows are snapped to the canonical allocation — the same figures a fresh import would produce.

The reason is drift. Scaling values already rounded to the cent does not land on the cent-exact allocation of the scaled total, so without snapping a long chain of scenarios would accumulate fractions of a cent and slowly stop being even at all. With it, the chain is stable:

chain <- ragged
for (i in 1:12) {
  chain <- build_scenario(chain, edits = list(scale = 1.37), name = paste0("s", i))
}
back <- build_scenario(chain, edits = list(total = 100000), name = "back to 100k")

identical(back@data$planned_spend, ragged@data$planned_spend)
#> [1] TRUE

The snap only touches flights already even to within a rounding tolerance, moves at most a cent between weeks, and never changes a flight’s total. A hand-shaped flight is left exactly as the planner set it.

The rate is what survives an edit

Spend is the common currency — the one quantity every channel shares — so it stays mandatory. A line item may also record what it buys, how much, and at what price, bound by one identity:

planned_spend = planned_units * planned_rate / rate_per(unit_type)

Supply any two and the third is computed, whichever way you actually have it. All three are then stored and the validator enforces the identity, so they cannot drift apart.

The question that shapes everything else is: when spend changes, which of the other two gives way? A negotiated CPM does not improve because the budget was cut. So the rate holds and the units follow:

social <- media_plan_from_df(
  data.frame(week = as.Date("2026-07-06"), channel = "Social", unit_type = "impression",
             planned_spend = 140000, planned_rate = 5),
  grain = "channel", time = "week", name = "Social"
)

cut <- build_scenario(social, edits = list(delta = -40000), name = "trimmed")
cut@data[, c("planned_spend", "planned_units", "planned_rate")]
#>   planned_spend planned_units planned_rate
#> 1         1e+05         2e+07            5

That is one rule, applied wherever money moves — through scaling, through a flight spreading across its weeks, through calendarize(). Had units been the invariant instead, every one of those places would have needed its own rule for keeping units in step.

Units add up only within one unit type. Across a mix, roll_up() keeps the spend and reports no units, because a total that adds GRPs to clicks is a number nobody should act on — and the spend is exactly what a common currency is for.

Scenarios are forks

A scenario is a new plan derived from another. The original is never modified — MediaPlan uses value semantics for exactly this reason. If deriving mutated the parent, the thing you are comparing against would change underneath you.

before <- sum(plan@data$planned_spend)
s <- build_scenario(plan, edits = list(scale = 2), name = "double")
after <- sum(plan@data$planned_spend)

c(before = before, after = after, unchanged = identical(before, after))
#>    before     after unchanged 
#>    110000    110000         1

Every derivation records its parent, so lineage chains:

s2 <- build_scenario(s, edits = list(scale = 0.5), name = "back down")
identical(s@parent_id, plan@id)
#> [1] TRUE
identical(s2@parent_id, s@id)
#> [1] TRUE

Ids are opaque on purpose. They exist for identity and lineage; human meaning lives in @name, @nickname and @objective. They are not yet an external join contract, so do not build one on them.

Status is not inherited

@status moves through a fixed vocabulary:

status_levels()
#> [1] "in development" "to review"      "approved"

A scenario derived from an approved plan is not itself approved. Carrying that forward would manufacture an approval nobody gave, so it resets:

approved <- media_plan_from_df(
  data.frame(week = as.Date("2026-07-06"), channel = "TV", planned_spend = 100000),
  grain = "channel", time = "week", name = "Signed off", status = "approved"
)

child <- build_scenario(approved, edits = list(scale = 1.5), name = "variant")
c(parent = approved@status, child = child@status)
#>           parent            child 
#>       "approved" "in development"

advertiser and planner are inherited — they describe the engagement and the person working, not the individual scenario.

A revision is a fact about lineage

Planners say Rev 3. An earlier version of this package stored that as a number on the plan, and it was the wrong thing to store: it had to be set by hand, and it restarted at 1 on every derivation, while Rev 3 means “the third version anyone approved” of a plan that may have been derived dozens of times in between.

So nothing is stored but the approval itself – status = "approved" and, optionally, the date it was given. The revision is derived from the lineage: an approved plan’s place among the approved plans on its branch.

rev2 <- revise(build_scenario(approved, edits = list(scale = 1.1), name = "Rev 2"),
               status = "approved", approved_on = "2026-07-20")
draft <- build_scenario(rev2, edits = list(scale = 0.9), name = "draft")

set <- add_scenario(add_scenario(scenario_set(approved), rev2), draft)
lineage(set)[, c("scenario", "status", "revision", "current")]
#>     scenario         status revision current
#> 1 Signed off       approved        1   FALSE
#> 2      Rev 2       approved        2    TRUE
#> 3      draft in development       NA   FALSE

The current approved plan is the one nothing approved has been derived from since – the one the agency is buying against. Two approvals on parallel branches are both current, and the package says so rather than guess which one won; an approval date says when someone signed, not which plan replaced which.

A scenario records how it was made

Every derived plan carries the edits that produced it, as @edits, and optionally why, as @rationale – who proposed it (a person, an agent, an optimizer), toward what goal, under which constraints.

The record is not a log written beside the edit. build_scenario() first turns whatever it was given into a canonical record – ops with their fields in a fixed order and dates as text on the plan’s clock, or an allocation as given – and then derives the scenario by replaying that record. What is stored is, by construction, exactly what was applied; replaying it on the parent reproduces the scenario to the last cent.

s3 <- build_scenario(plan, name = "move", edits = op_transfer(
  10000, from = list(channel = "TV"), to = list(channel = "Search")))
s3@edits
#> $form
#> [1] "ops"
#> 
#> $ops
#> $ops[[1]]
#> $ops[[1]]$transfer
#> [1] 10000
#> 
#> $ops[[1]]$from
#> $ops[[1]]$from$channel
#> [1] "TV"
#> 
#> 
#> $ops[[1]]$to
#> $ops[[1]]$to$channel
#> [1] "Search"

That is also why a transfer is one operation rather than two deltas. “Move 10k from TV to Search” is one intent; written as a cut and an addition, the record would hold two unrelated changes, and nothing would say they belonged together.

Some money cannot move

A real plan is not all free to edit. An upfront commitment is fixed; a partner minimum is a floor; some lines are capped. Each row may carry min_spend and max_spend to say so, and every edit respects them:

held <- media_plan_from_df(
  data.frame(month = as.Date("2026-10-01"),
             channel = c("Streaming", "Search", "Social"),
             planned_spend = c(60000, 20000, 10000),
             min_spend = c(60000, 15000, NA),
             max_spend = c(60000, NA, NA)),
  grain = "channel", time = "month", name = "Held"
)

build_scenario(held, edits = list(delta = -8000), name = "trim")@data[
  , c("channel", "planned_spend", "min_spend")]
#>     channel planned_spend min_spend
#> 1 Streaming         60000     60000
#> 2    Search         15000     15000
#> 3    Social          7000        NA

The cut of 8,000 spread in proportion across the rows that could give, until Search reached its floor; Social took the rest, and Streaming – committed – did not move. That is what an edit across a group does: rows at a bound stop there and the rest take up the slack. An edit that names each row’s value outright (set, scale, delta_each, an optimizer’s allocation) cannot be redistributed, so a row it would push past a bound refuses it instead.

Only the two bounds are stored. Whether a row is committed (floor and cap both equal its spend), has a floor, or is capped is derived from them every time, for the same reason the flight window is: a label stored beside the numbers could disagree with them, and a derived one cannot.

Bounds change through one operation, rebound, and never as a side effect of moving money. To cut committed spend, lower the commitment and then cut, in that order, in one edits list – so the record says that both happened.

Rules about one row, rules about many

Spend bounds are rules about one row, and they live in the plan because an edit can keep them: spreading a cut across a group, it can see each row’s floor and stop there.

A rule about many rows is different. “Streaming keeps at least 40% of the plan” depends on everything else in the plan – a transfer between two other channels can break it without touching Streaming at all. No single edit can enforce it row by row, so it is not enforced; it is checked. Such rules are kept apart, in a PlanConstraints, and check_constraints() measures a plan against them:

rules <- plan_constraints(list(
  rule_min_share(0.7, target = list(channel = "Streaming"))
), name = "share floor")

check_constraints(held, rules)[, c("type", "target", "actual", "limit", "ok")]
#> Warning: 1 of 2 rule(s) violated: min_share 0.7 on channel Streaming: actual
#> 0.6667 (slack -0.0333).
#>         type            target actual limit    ok
#> 1  min_share channel Streaming 0.6667   0.7 FALSE
#> 2 row_bounds       (every row) 0.0000   0.0  TRUE

A broken group rule is reported with a warning, never refused: the plan is legal, and whoever approves it needs to see what it breaks. Keeping the rules in one object, rather than in each caller’s head, is what lets an agent checking its own proposal and an optimizer searching for a better one hold the plan to the same definition of “allowed”.

Spend has a basis

The same plan can be stated as media net (what the media costs), client net (what the client pays, fees included) or gross. @spend_basis declares which one the figures are:

revise(held, spend_basis = "media_net")@spend_basis
#> [1] "media_net"

It is a declaration, never a conversion. Turning media net into client net means applying a fee schedule, and fee schedules differ by contract and by channel; that belongs with the caller. What the package does with the basis is refuse to combine plans that disagree – a scenario set, or a subplan beneath its parent – because comparing media net with client net would report the fees as a change in plan.

Comparison unions the cells

compare_scenarios(level = "cell") compares over the union of grain cells across the whole set, zero-filling where a scenario has no row.

This is invisible when scenarios come from build_scenario(), since those always inherit the parent’s exact row set. It matters when scenarios are authored independently — one workbook tab each, say — because then their row sets need not match:

a <- media_plan_from_df(
  data.frame(week = as.Date("2026-07-06"), channel = c("TV", "Search"), planned_spend = c(80000, 40000)),
  grain = "channel", time = "week", name = "Plan", nickname = "baseline"
)
b <- media_plan_from_df(
  data.frame(week = as.Date("2026-07-06"), channel = "TV", planned_spend = 120000),   # Search dropped entirely
  grain = "channel", time = "week", name = "Plan", nickname = "no search"
)

compare_scenarios(add_scenario(scenario_set(a), b), "cell")
#>    scenario channel       week planned_spend share_of_total spend_vs_base
#> 1  baseline      TV 2026-07-06         80000      0.6666667             0
#> 2  baseline  Search 2026-07-06         40000      0.3333333             0
#> 3 no search      TV 2026-07-06        120000      1.0000000         40000
#> 4 no search  Search 2026-07-06             0      0.0000000        -40000

Search appears for no search as a −40,000 delta, not as a missing row. Without the union, a cut would simply vanish from the table — totals would still reconcile, and the reader would see money appearing from nowhere.

What lives elsewhere

mediaplanr does not fit models, forecast, or optimize. Its only imports are S7 and jsonlite, plus base R’s stats and utils.

         mediaplanr                       mrmopt
  ┌────────────────────────┐   ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │ plan object, grain,    │   │ response curves, fitting,│
  │ validation, lineage,   │   │ forecasting, budget      │
  │ scenarios, comparison  │   │ optimization (opt_mix)   │
  └────────────────────────┘   └──────────────────────────┘
                ↘                   ↙
                  a caller wires them

An earlier revision did include a forecast() and a budget optimizer. Both were removed, for reasons worth stating so they are not rebuilt by accident:

  • The consuming application already called mrmopt::opt_mix(), so the in-package optimizer was a weaker second implementation.
  • Implementing forecast() forced a modelling decision into a container: response curves have a non-zero lower asymptote, so “predicted volume” is ambiguous, and the package had to pick a convention. That belongs where the modelling is owned.
  • It inverted the dependency. A ScenarioSet could not exist without a set of fitted models, so plans could not be held or compared without them.

An allocation computed by an optimizer re-enters through the same door a hand edit uses:

result <- mrmopt::opt_mix(models, budget = 160000)
alloc  <- data.frame(channel = result$solution$channel,
                     planned_spend = result$solution$optimal_spend)

build_scenario(base, edits = alloc, name = "Optimized",
               objective = "max KPI at 160k, opt_mix point method")

The package never learns where the numbers came from. @objective is where you record why.
